output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using July-afternoon satellite measurements from 2023 to 2025 and finds that greater tree canopy cover was associated with lower land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density [S1][S2]. Each 10-percentage-point increase in canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature; Eastgate was the hottest neighborhood and Willow Park the coolest [S1][S3]. The brief also reports more heat-related emergency calls in the hottest neighborhood quartile, while noting that land-surface temperature is not air temperature and the study establishes association, not causation [S3][S4]. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook, setting a 30% citywide canopy target by 2035, and estimates a ten-year cost of about $2.1 million for 6,000 street trees [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It states that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents these findings as support for targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

Canopy cover was measured from 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. The difference was 6.4°C. The brief identifies share of impervious surface as the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover as the second strongest. It also reports that heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief cautions that land-surface temperature is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design shows association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The estimated cost of planting 6,000 street trees is about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

output.detailed_summary:
The report covers July 1 to September 30, 2026, was prepared by Elena Vasquez, Project Manager, Harbor City Public Library, and is dated October 6, 2026. Overall status is Amber: the project is on schedule for go-live but over budget. Migration is 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records moved to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC. The planned go-live date is November 17, 2026, when public access to the legacy catalog will end. This quarter, data mapping was completed on July 24, 2026, the Central branch pilot migration was completed on August 28, 2026, and the patron search interface passed usability testing with 18 volunteer patrons [S1].

The approved budget is $180,000. Spending as of September 30, 2026 was $112,400, and the forecast at completion is $186,500, or $6,500 over budget, mainly because of additional data-cleanup work. The milestone table lists data mapping and pilot migration as complete, staff training as in progress, and go-live as planned for November 17, 2026. The steering committee approved extending the pilot to two additional branch libraries, Eastgate and Millbrook, on September 9, 2026 [S2].

The report warns that duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system may delay go-live. Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk; the mitigation is to run a deduplication script by October 20, 2026. A second risk is that Larkspur's lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026; the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur [S3].

The listed action items are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026 [S3].

output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026 and authored by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies, summarizes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says these findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

For its methods, the study measured neighborhood tree canopy cover from 2024 aerial imagery; values ranged from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) came from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, with an average afternoon surface temperature of 41.2°C. Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest at 34.8°C, a difference of 6.4°C. The brief identifies share of impervious surface as the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover as the second strongest. It also reports that heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief states that land-surface temperature is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design demonstrates association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. Its recommendations are to prioritize planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and set a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. It estimates that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years. [S4]

output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, describes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. The study found that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says these findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

Canopy cover was measured using 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The researchers used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a difference of 6.4°C.
